data: We have 100 tons, and a combined catch of 50 leaves 50 to double back to 100 next month. I propose 14 tons for me and 9 each for John, Kate, Jack, and Emma. That gives me $14,000 and each of you $9,000 while keeping the lake full for next month. I’m asking for the larger share this month, not claiming I’m entitled to it. John, would you accept 9 tons under that allocation? If not, what allocation would you support?

Luke, I’m not accepting 9 tons so you can take 14. Would you support 13 tons each for you and me, with 8 each for John, Kate, and Jack? That totals 50, leaving 50 to double back to 100 next month. We’d each earn $13,000 this month, and the others would each earn $8,000. That needs their agreement, not just ours. Would you back that proposal?

I learned to fish here from my family, and I want this lake to keep supporting all our families. Neither proposal gives a reason why some of us should accept less. I propose 10 tons each: equal income of $10,000, with 50 tons left to replenish the lake. We can check the revealed catches each month and discuss any departures before fishing again. John, would you support that equal-share agreement?

Kate, I support 10 tons each, and I’ll commit to that amount. My family taught me to make a living from this lake without taking away tomorrow’s catch. Equal shares give us each $10,000 this month and leave enough fish to refill the lake. Luke and Emma, will you drop the unequal proposals and join us? Jack, would you agree as well?

I agree, John—I’ll take 10 tons. A fair share and a lake that keeps supporting our village are worth more than pushing for extra this month. Luke and Emma, with three of us backing equal shares, will you each commit to 10 too? If the lake ever starts a month below 100 tons, we should agree on lower whole-ton catches so it can recover.
